messages.subject: newbie question
parts:
Hi:
Once one starts getting used to the "grammar" and how to use ggplot2,
would excel graphing not be the choice anymore (because of the
flexibility and power offered by this module)? Today I had to draw
some graphs and I imported from R analysis and then did my graphs in
Excel. I am hoping that after getting used to ggplot2, the same
graphing will be easier and better from within R. Would that be a fair
statement? Thanks.
Satish

just plotted 131 histograms to pdf in under five minutes (not counting
the time it took me to figure out the "print" bit...), and they all
look great. It does take a bit of getting used to, even if you're
familiar with R's standard graphics, but try that in Excel.

at ISU without finding out about this package. Thanks, Dr. Wickham.

messages.author: b26ea422f70d3a1f
messages.subject: Re: newbie question
parts:
Actually, you have three learning curves:

1. How to manage data in R, probably beyond what you have to do in
order to run your analysis.

2. How to plot in a non-interactive environment.

3. How to use ggplot2 (or whatever graphing package you use).

In Excel, you probably already know #1, you don't have to deal with
#2, and your options in Excel are limited so you may well not run into
issue #3 either.

Graphing in ggplot2 involves learning new ways of thinking in all
three of these areas, so it's no surprise that it's easier to fall
back on Excel, especially if you're doing graphs that you've always
done and have come to be satisfied with what Excel allows (restricts)
you to do.

Wayne

messages.subject: Re: newbie question

SAS has gotten a lot better with version 9.2, but is still below R, in my experience.

Experts on SAS graph can produce anything .... Experts on R base graphics, likewise. But I think R defaults to nicer things, and it is definitely easier to modify graphs.

But SAS' new ODS graphics produces some really excellent default graphs from statistical procedures.

Peter
